Ukrainian winter: how bad could it get?

It’s pretty clear that Russian President Vladimir Putin will attempt to destroy what is left of Ukraine’s power sector this winter. In fact, the campaign has already started: last year’s bombardment got under way in September; this year’s arguably already started at the end of July.

Russia is increasingly targeting energy and power assets. Not that you’d notice as Bankova, Ukraine’s presidential administration, is focusing on the residential strikes and tragic loss of life in Kyiv as entire families are being killed every day.

Of course, this is perfectly understandable as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy is hoping to guilt-trip reluctant allies into giving him desperately needed interceptors and more resources. While Kyiv features prominently in the “Russia is a terrorist state” headlines, the real focus of the war is in Odesa and the Fortress Belt cities of the Donbas and the important casualties are DTEK and Naftogaz – though of course I don’t want to belittle the horrible civilian casualties’ reports.

However, I'm surprised at how little detailed reporting there is on just how much damage the power sector has taken since the war started. In 2022, Ukraine had about 59GW of installed capacity, (of which 22GW was thermal, 28GW hydro and 13.8GW was nuclear).

Going into last year’s winter campaign, Ukraine only had 14GW left with a winter demand of around 17GW. In a rare, detailed comment on the sector Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said yesterday that every single one of Ukraine’s power stations has suffered some sort of damage.

There was about a 3GW deficit in generating capacity last year, but the Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal admitted that in the first half of this year another 2GW has been taken out so the deficit is now on the order of 5GW.

And that is before the Russian winter bombardment has got going. Putin is reportedly stockpiling missiles after missile production capacity doubled last year and according to reports the full year production targets have already been hit. Mr P is not mucking about. This year’s attack is going to be devastating.

You’ll notice that the remain capacity is about the same as the nuclear power plant (NPP) generating capacity as obviously Russia can’t blow up the likes of Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant (ZNPP) as would cause an off-the-scale environmental disaster and, more importantly, almost certainly wreck Moscow’s relationship with Beijing, which has been pretty clear on its ban on doing anything nuclear.

But that doesn’t mean nuclear power will stay on the grid. As we reported last autumn, Russia also has the option of taking out the ultra-high voltage 750kV substations – pay attention as I'm sure you will be hearing a lot more about these after the summer is over.

These are especially large substations and are in effect the backbone of the Ukrainian grid. So far, Russia has largely ignored them, as part of Putin’s use of war as a political tool to try and force Zelenskiy to capitulate, but when it took out Odesa's substation last October it plunged the entire region into darkness for a week. As they are a Soviet-legacy piece of infrastructure, they are also very hard to repair or replace as no one makes parts for them.

Now imagine if Russia uses its highly accurate, and now unstoppable, ballistic missiles to target the substations. Even if only half of them were destroyed, bringing Ukraine’s available generation capacity down to 6GW that would blow out the power deficit to over 10GW – an impossible gap to close. And Shmyhal said last week, Bankova is afraid that Russia will also target water and sewage infrastructure. You can live in an apartment with -10°C indoor temperatures – many Kyivian residents did it last year by putting up tents in their living rooms  – but how long can you live without running water or working toilets?

Once you start digging into the details you can see why Zelenskiy is starting to look so desperate. There is very little he can do to stop it. US President Donald Trump has flip flopped on the Patriot licensing rights, which is reportedly being blocked by the leading US arms makers who are afraid of losing their profits to Ukraine (!).

There are also several hundred interceptors in Europe (remember Zelenskiy also asked Trump for 300 to get through the winter), but as we reported, and Politicoconfirmed last week, those European governments are refusing to give them up – Spain and Greece in particular which have the most.

Greece is not turning out to be a good friend of Ukraine’s, is it? Athens also blocked the 21stsanctions package until it got an exemption from the oil price cap sanctions and Greek tankers just exported a record amount of oil from Russia, helping to fill the Kremlin’s war coffers… And they said Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban was a good friend of Russia’s.

Trump was also badgered into promising to send Ukraine interceptor missiles “every month”. But no one has put a number on that. I strongly suspect the Pentagon is only intending to send new ones as they roll off the conveyor belt – about five a month – so at least keep its depleted stockpile stable. Given Russia is capable of firing five ballistic missiles a day that is not going to make any difference at all. Russia fired an estimated 900 missiles (not counting drones) at Ukraine last year, according to Center for Strategic & International Studies (CSIS). This year that number could easily double.

Another detail that is not getting enough attention is just how much damage Ukraine’s long distance “sanctions” (as Zelenskiy refers to drone strikes now) actually do to Russia’s refineries. But this is more excusable, as obviously neither the Kremlin nor the companies are keen to share this information. But what is becoming clear is that as the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) switches targets from oil refineries to warehouses, many of Russia’s circa 35 refineries that have been hit – and all of them have now been hit – are affecting repairs and at least partially coming back online. The fuel crisis has clearly passed peak and petrol stations are starting to open again. That is also partly thanks to supplies coming from Belarus, Kazakhstan and especially India.

India is another one that has turned out to be especially chummy with the Kremlin, but you can understand that too. As an ex-colony, it has not been particularly well treated by the Trump administration and has a growing resentment for the Western neo-colonial treatment it still gets whenever it goes to the West for help, like in last year’s short war with Pakistan.

Meduza had an interesting go at assessing the damage to Russian refineries by referring to infrared satellite maps in an article today, which concluded what was already assumed: Ukrainian drones are not powerful enough to destroy refineries, but can do serious damage to some of their more sensitive equipment that puts them out of action for months. But the bottom line is, Ukraine doesn’t have the destructive firepower to collapse the Russian economy or force Putin into negotiations in a position of weakness.

So, what does Ukraine with only 6GW in the depths of winter look like? It’s hard to say definitely, especially given the Ukrainian population managed to tough out last year’s attempt to freeze it into submission, but we are probably talking about an electricity emergency approaching a humanitarian crisis, particularly in the large cities.

Ukrainian winter peak electricity demand has been around 16.5–18GW, and the IEA says a cold winter can push demand to 18GW or more. So, 6GW of available/operational generation capacity would cover only roughly one-third of unconstrained peak demand. Even adding the present 2.1GW winter import capability from the EU would leave Ukraine with perhaps 8.1GW against demand of 18GW – about half of what is needed.

The state would be forced to ration electricity heavily and protect critical loads: hospitals, water and sewage pumping (if they are not destroyed too), telecommunications, military facilities, railways, district-heating systems and other essential infrastructure. Households and ordinary businesses would absorb a disproportionate share of extensive rolling blackouts that could extend to 12-18 hours a day for residential.

And that assumes the substations survive. If they are knocked out then the blackouts will be complete and could last for days or even weeks.

Electricity itself isn't necessarily the greatest danger. The lack of heat and water are. One of the big dangers is that if the power to a building is gone, you have to turn the water off, even if Russia doesn’t target the pumping stations, otherwise the water will freeze and burst their pipes – serious damage that can’t be repaired until spring, when the whole system has to be rebuilt.

Where is the cut off? Last year residents could cope with 6–10-hour daily blackouts. With 12–18-hour blackouts you get serious economic and social disruption, but there are some work arounds like generators. However, with only 2–6 hours of electricity per day the cities will begin to be unliveable as apartments become too cold to inhabit and things like water have to be shut off completely and drained from the buildings. Those who can, will leave the city for the dacha or leave the country. Iuliia Mendel, Zelenskiy’s former press secretary, has already reported on traffic jams at the borders as some people are already leaving in anticipation of what might come.

I'm not saying this will happen. Ukrainians have demonstrated extraordinary resilience and the ability to function through last year’s blackouts. But this is a very real scenario that is lurking behind Zelenskiy's frenetic diplomatic outreach at the moment. Ukraine is not ready to repel a large Russian missile bombardment and its partners are either unwilling, but mostly, unable to do much to help it at this point.

@Elonmusk, regarding relevancy and shadow banning: 

I think you should let the populace block who they don’t want to listen to, and not the algorithm actively blocking you, because 200–500 active accounts did, even if they may be bots or paid users. 

This then creates a negative incentive to harm and harass others if you have the numbers. If this is a public square, let it be one. 

If there’s a man on the street with a sign, only those who choose to pay attention see him; but when the negative incentive is applied, he exists, but others don’t see him. 

So, personal active blocking is more accurate to the public square you talk about—that’s actually free.

 I mean, porn sites are still accessible because of personal choice, no matter how much a large proportion of the population speak negatively  of them because they’re largely a personal choice.

For instance, WhatsApp status posts or chats are not tampered with. If I hide anything, it stays hidden for me and only me. So first the system needs to respect individual taste by simply letting people choose and block who they don’t want to see.

 Only after that should it start showing what users are actually interested in. Right now it feels like the platform is controlling what people see, not for protection, but to keep information away from them.

Looking at the most recent public algorithm (xai-org/x-algorithm), the exact places that need fixing are clear. The Phoenix model predicts how likely someone is to block, mute, report, or hit “not interested.”

RankingScorer then multiplies those predictions by heavy negative weights (report around –234, mute around –58.8, not interested around –43.2, block around –31.2).

Real reports and blocks also feed into labeling systems and visibility filters that can bury posts more widely, especially for people who don’t follow the author.

That’s how a relatively small group can tank reach and create the incentive to harass. 

The hard personal filter already in the code — AuthorSocialgraphFilter — is the right piece. It just removes posts from accounts you blocked or muted. 

Everything that predicts negatives ahead of time or turns other people’s actions into reduced visibility for everyone else is the problem.

Here’s how a real public square that can’t be controlled by any government or body would actually work. It would be run only by the people who individually choose to listen or not.

Start with individual taste as the foundation. Let every user block or mute whoever/ideas they don’t want to see. 

Those choices stay local/user. The algorithm then learns your preferences — both positive and negative — only from what you do: likes, replies, time spent, shares, follows, and also hides, mutes, blocks, and “not interested.” From that it builds a Preferences feed that matches your taste. 

Other people’s reports don’t get to decide what shows up for you.
Then give people clean, separate views they control:

•  A pure Following feed that only shows posts from the people you chose to follow.

•  A Similar-to-Following layer that brings in accounts and posts that feel like the ones you already follow.

•  Exploration modes you turn on when you want them: mainstream or trending, and location views (India, Nigeria, Australia or cities like , Benin, Toronto). 

These stay separate and still respect your blocks and mutes. They don’t quietly leak into your other feeds.

Add real transparency on reputation. Instead of an invisible algorithm quietly burying posts because of hidden reports, put a public reputation section on each post. 

Anyone can see it’s been reported, how many times, and the stated reasons. The original poster gets a clear public space to respond and defend it. 

Reputation and ranking then rise or fall based on what people can actually read and judge for themselves. 

Coordinated or fake reports become visible and easy to challenge. Good defenses become visible too. The public decides.

Under this setup no outside body can quietly control the square. The only way a voice disappears from your view is if you remove it. 

There’s no payoff for mass-reporting someone just to shut them up. Visibility is the default.

Suppression is personal and explicit. Your feed learns from your own + and – signals. 

Exploration is something you choose.

Reputation is a 2 sided sword.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

How Modi Managed “THE MEDIA” To Stay In Power

In 2002, Gujarat CM Narendra Modi sat in front of a BBC camera and admitted his one real weakness:
“One area where I was very, very weak… that was how to handle the media.”

He never forgot that lesson. He just decided the media should never be allowed to become a problem again.

Between March and July, the government sent one blocking order every 68 seconds to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube.

1.95 lakh orders in five months.
1,275 every single day.
Instagram — the platform students used during the Jantar Mantar protests — received more than 1 lakh of them.

The same playbook that started with ED and CBI cases against NDTV, the takeover of Network18, and UAPA against NewsClick’s founder is now running on autopilot through the Sahyog portal. Content vanishes in three hours. Often without anyone even seeing the order.

When dissent is treated as a security threat and protest as a crime, the media is no longer a watchdog. It is just another department to be controlled.
The 2002 admission was honest.

The 2026 response is the real story. 68 seconds.
That’s how long this government takes to silence you.
He admitted one weakness in 2002. He spent the next 24 years making sure it never happened again.

On the night of 14th August 1947, a flag flew on Jawaharlal Nehru's car as it went over Raisina Hill. It was the first time the tricolour we know today was ever flown.

That flag had been stitched under the supervision of a 28 year old woman.

Her name was Surayya Tyabji.

She was born in 1919 in Hyderabad. She was a painter. Her work was later shown in London and in Jakarta. She was married to Badruddin Tyabji, a civil servant who was part of the group working on what independent India would look like.

Everyone had assumed the flag was settled. Pingali Venkayya had designed the tricolour used by the Congress, with Gandhi's charkha in the middle. It had been carried through the freedom movement for over 20 years.

Then, weeks before independence, a problem was raised. That flag was a party flag. A country that was about to include everyone could not fly the symbol of one political party.

So the design had to be redone, quickly.

The Tyabjis were given the job.

They replaced the charkha with the Ashoka Chakra, the wheel from the Lion Capital of Ashoka at Sarnath. The reason was simple and deliberate. Ashoka belonged to all Indians, and to no party.

Their daughter Laila Tyabji has written the family's account of it. Her mother drew the graphic version. The printing press at the Viceregal Lodge made the impressions. Everyone approved.

The English historian Trevor Royle recorded in his book that the flag which flew on Nehru's car that night had been made by Tyabji's wife.

On 22nd July 1947 the design was accepted by the Constituent Assembly.

A report in the Times of India in January 1950 described that first flag as having been presented to the nation by the women of India at the midnight session of the Constituent Assembly on 14th August 1947.

Before the flag, the same couple had worked on the national emblem. Nehru asked Badruddin to do something about it because he had an eye for these things. Surayya drew the version of the 4 lions that has been on every Indian government document since.

She was 28 years old.

She died in 1978 in Mumbai.

Her daughter has said that neither of her parents ever felt they had designed the national emblem. They felt they had only reminded India of something that had always been part of its identity.

Official records of the Constituent Assembly do not name individual contributors, so most textbooks still credit only Venkayya, and his work genuinely came first.

But today, when the flag goes up, look at the wheel in the middle of it.

A young Muslim woman put it there, on purpose, so that no Indian would be left out of it.

IFF’s Statement on the Blocking of X Account of the Cockroach Janta Party

22 May 2026

On May 21, 2026, the X (formerly Twitter) handle of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) (@CJP_2029) was withheld in India under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. IFF strongly condemns the blocking of the CJP’s X handle as a blatant misuse of State power and an arbitrary and disproportionate attempt to stifle freedom of speech and expression, a fundamental right guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution of India.

According to reporting by The Indian Express on May 22, 2026, the blocking directions were issued on the basis of inputs from the Intelligence Bureau citing threat to the sovereignty of India, jeopardizing national security and the fact that the account was gaining traction among young people. Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000, empowers the Central government to direct any Government agency or intermediary to block public access to information in the “interest of sovereignty and integrity of India, defence of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States or public order or for preventing incitement to the commission of any cognizable offence”. While Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000 permits blocking on limited grounds, these grounds cannot be vague and speculative. Political commentary and criticism of public institutions are protected forms of speech under the Indian Constitution. The popularity of the account or the fact that the account mobilised young people through political expression cannot by itself be treated as a threat to national security.

The Indian Express’s report mentions that “blocking orders are issued under a confidential framework” which is deeply concerning. We remind the Union Government that the Supreme Court of India upheld Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000 in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) on the basis that it is a narrowly drawn provision with several safeguards in place, including written reasoning for the blocking that is subject to legal challenge. State censorship like the blocking of CJP’s X account propagates opacity and provides affected users with no options for redressal, thereby effectively defeating these safeguards. IFF calls on the Union government to ensure timely notices are provided to affected users along with clear grounds and avenues for remedy.

Other countries have adopted stronger safeguards. UN census principles emphasise that individual information should not be linked to other government databases for non-statistical purposes. Countries including Canada and Australia avoid collecting certain identifiers or keep contact information separate from statistical data. Germany’s Constitutional Court has also rejected census-to-register linkage. (7/8)

IFF supports the inclusion of caste in Census 2027. Reliable caste data can be essential to understanding inequality and advancing constitutional commitments to equality. But counting caste does not require creating identity-linked records. We have asked the government to delete unnecessary identifiers, guarantee that data will not be linked with other databases, publish security and retention safeguards, and make any retained fields expressly voluntary. (8/8)
